pitch_detail.notes: Easy climbing in four short sections: a wide dihedral or chimney for about 20 ft to a big ledge, past a bulge, then slightly left into a fat dihedral and squeeze chimney to a second large ledge (a two-bolt rap anchor sits on the right). A short chimney above leads to a third ledge with a gear-only belay, so bring small and medium cams to build it. Roughly 130 to 140 ft in all.

Follow the obvious double crack system; after about 20 ft the left crack passes a bolt and heads off as a neighbouring route, while the right crack is the original line. Big cams (doubles of the largest size help) and some leap-frogging make it easier, and medium to large stoppers protect the upper part. Large loose blocks shift near the top, so face climb around them for the last 25 ft. Belay on a ledge at bolts.

The crux pitch: mostly wide climbing, but the protection is mostly narrower than the climbing. Bolts protect the offwidth and the hard moves at its start, and the first one is not inspiring, so get gear in as well. Past the crux a squeeze chimney offers a secure stance, with gear deep inside; the polished face holds outside are an alternative for those who do not fit. Roughly 100 to 110 ft. Sources differ on the number of bolts, and the grade is quoted as 5.9 by some and 5.9+ by others.

Pick one of two ways: a 5.7 face on the right that needs a short traverse on hands or feet, or a chimney on the left at about the same grade, which suits a nervous follower better. At roughly 80 ft it is much shorter than pitches 2 and 3, and it stops at a two-bolt anchor a few feet under the top.

pitch_detail.notes: Easy start with two good bolts to the anchor. Pitches 1 and 2 can be climbed as one 170 ft pitch, so a 60 m rope is helpful.
From the bolt anchor, take the right-facing desert-varnished dihedral for about 60 ft, then move left to the belay anchors.
Keep following the fine crack, stemming where it helps, for about 120 ft to the next bolted station. Expect the varnished rock to feel slick.
Leave the anchor rightward onto the arching crack and take it to the last bolted station, tucked under the huge roof. On the descent, watch that the ropes do not wedge in this same crack.

pitch_detail.notes: Shared with the neighbouring route. Small corners facing right lead up to a crack; the ground is easy enough that some parties solo it, others place a few pieces, to the bolted station.

A bolt line goes directly up the face. Holds are mostly incut edges, with a handful of slopers and moves that ask for balance. Ends at bolts. Some parties rate this the route's hardest pitch. When descending, use the rappel station off to the left, not this belay.
More of the same straight above, on edges and with plenty of bolts; a couple of pieces of gear fit the crack near the start. Ends at bolts.
Similar to the pitch below but slightly easier.
The angle eases toward slab, and the gaps between bolts grow in places. Ends at the station under the last pitch.

The crux comes immediately, between the belay and the second bolt. Incut edges give way to smooth slab split by a faint, shallow crack, taken on tiny holds and smears. The first bolt is a stretch, and falling before it can swing you onto the belayer. Higher up the edges come back, the difficulty drops, and the route finishes at a roomy ledge, the one belay on the climb where you are not hanging.

pitch_detail.notes: Take a 5.6 crack that angles up and left; one spot is better protected with a large cam. Many parties stop at a two-bolt anchor about 110 ft up, though a 60 m rope reaches the next bolted station on a ledge to the right. Avoid wandering left into the gully, which has only gear belays. Beyond, a huge terrace slants up and right; walk to its top. It is third class apart from perhaps the opening move, and many parties keep the rope on.
Aim for the tree at the top of a gully. A short awkward boulder-problem start off the ground, then easier going up the gully to the tree, about 70 ft.
Here the angle steepens. A thin crack splits a dark face; take it, move left beneath a roof, then stay with a second crack to its end at a block wrapped in slings, about 150 ft.

Bolts visible above the belay mark a harder direct variation (5.10d). The normal way goes down from the belay and traverses right around the corner to the base of a crack in the centre of a black wall, about 50 ft.

Follow the crack, move right to a bolt, and continue up a face with some runout to a station on two bolts, about 100 ft. A 50 m rope can link pitches 5 and 6, though drag makes the last runout moves harder. Most parties go down from this station instead of carrying on to the top.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 130 ft to the slung block at the top of pitch 4, or split it into 50 ft to an intermediate bolted anchor on the direct variation and then 80 ft to the block.
hazards: heavy rope drag and knobs that catch the rope
do not rappel to the bolts about 120 ft down to the right: parties have had severe rope drag there

rappel_detail.notes: A 140 ft rappel reaches the tree that ends pitch 3. Another option is to rappel a little left onto the broad Lunch Ledge and scramble clockwise across exposed rock to the next tree used for rappelling.
rappel_detail.station: The slung round block at the top of pitch 4.

rappel_detail.notes: A 70 ft rappel lands on a broad, broken ledge system. Pick the simplest line down from there to a huge level ledge; the final step down is onto a cheater block. Then walk right to bolts on the up-canyon face of a large detached block for the next rappel.
hazards: stepping down onto the cheater block is awkward; give beginners a belay

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel about 150 ft to the ground, angling a little right (north). Intermediate anchors about 50 ft down in an alcove let you split it into two shorter rappels.
hazards: bad rope drag when pulling the full-length rappel
unknown whether a single 60 m rope reaches the ground from the intermediate anchor; a 70 m does
rappel_detail.station: Bolts on the up-canyon side of the huge free-standing block, the top of the second pitch. A second bolted station lies left of the cheater block.

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the creek bed and clip bolts up to a large ledge, then a few more bolts lead on to a ledge with bushes, about 165 ft.
Head up and left into a chimney, exit on its right, and follow easier ground to the foot of the large chimney on the right flank of the Black Tower. A long pitch; the rope may need to stretch.

The centrepiece: a smooth, wide crack climbed as a chimney, well protected, for about 140 ft to a bolted station on a ledge on the right-hand wall. Haul the pack on a long sling through the chimneys instead of wearing it.

Chimney higher, moving left where the crack pinches down, then easier ground to a ledge. Beyond it a slimmer chimney starts at a fixed nut and has two bolts that are easy to miss; climb out from the chimney's back to spot them. If the rope reaches, belay on top of the Black Tower; if not, stop where the chimney ends and add a short, easy pitch to the top of the tower. The bottom of the chimney can be bypassed to the right.
Above the tower's top, take the face through an overhang and head for a ledge with brush on it.
Traverse easily right to the Elephant's Trunk and climb it to a ledge at its top.
Climb the crack, with a few bolts along it, to a bolted station on a ledge. Rappels descend directly below this point. It can be linked with the previous pitch.

Stay in the same crack for about 400 ft in all, belaying at each bolted station. On pitch 10, traverse a short way right past a bolt to a small roof, then a second roof that is a bit harder; protection is good and there are big holds above and to the left of the crack. Some of the finest climbing on the route.

pitch_detail.notes: The most physical pitch. An off-width that narrows to fists climbs over a bulge, then a thin, strenuous hand crack slants right to a little roof. Over the roof is a brief wide stretch, then a hand crack closing down to fingers ends at a bolted belay on a ledge.
Jam past a bulge into a finger crack, move right into a wider section, then take a hand crack that narrows to fingers up to a ledge with three bolts. It is often linked with pitch 1.

The hardest moves. Move right and jam thin cracks up to a horizontal, then a long finger crack to a pod; from there finger and hand cracks lead left over two small bulges to a ledge belay on two bolts. A 0.5-size cam is the awkward size to have here.
A corner and a series of ledges trend right over somewhat sandy rock, then the line returns left to a roomy ledge with two bolts. A bolt protects the second.

Two finishes. The regular left finish climbs a short corner, hand-traverses left to an off-width in a dihedral, then traverses left under a roof (about 5.7 and airy) to the summit. Use plenty of slings against rope drag, or split the pitch in two. The direct right finish climbs the corner and then face moves past four bolts at 5.11a.

pitch_detail.notes: Two pitches usually led as one, roughly 160 ft. The opening bolt sits around nine feet up, so bring a stick-clip or a boost.
About 70 ft to a comfortable ledge, a usual place to stop for the night when fixing the lower pitches.
The Wrinkles. Pendulum out to the right and tension traverse back to the left in a series; once the good placements end, head left. This is the hardest aid of the route.
A good crack leads through the arching roof.
Follow a crack to a short bolt ladder.
A left-facing corner with a few trickier moves, ending at a decent stance below the last aid pitch. Tricam placements between bolt ladders on the upper pitches have flared out and held poorly.
Continue up the corner system, then pendulum left into another corner. The pitch ends on a large, dirty, sandy, down-sloping ledge with loose material, so move carefully.
Free climb a low-angle chimney full of loose debris, then a chute of loose sand, rock and plant matter. The belay is at a pair of good trees.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin a few metres right of the large boulder at the foot of the buttress. A low-angle crack with a tree in it crosses the face to a two-bolt station below a short chimney holding a 6-10 inch crack.
Climb the chimney (a #4 Camalot low, or a #2 higher), then the slab above past five bolts.

Step right to a crack, climb it about 20 ft, then step left onto a slab with three bolts. A 5.11 variation steps sharply left past two bolts into a water groove and past one more bolt before rejoining the slab.
Clip a bolt out left, go around the corner, and climb the slab past two bolts. The last stretch to the anchor is run out.
Clip the first bolt, climb right to the arete and past a couple of bolts, then make a long reach up and left to a ledge with a two-bolt anchor. Belaying here reduces rope drag.
Climb about 20 ft to the first bolt, traverse right about 15 ft to a hard-to-see bolt, and continue right over a ridge. The zig-zag line causes drag even with long draws.

The crux. Climb up to a finger crack and an undercling and clip a bolt, then move around onto the steep right side, underclinging past about 11 bolts before going straight up. It aids easily, and some think the hard section is best aided.
Long, sustained climbing past nine or ten bolts, with a hard move left into a groove worn by water, then the ground eases.
Slabs about 30 m up and left to a single bolt roughly 20 ft out left of the direct line, then up and right about 20 m to a new two-bolt anchor. Can be simul-climbed.
Continue up slab climbing past one bolt to a new two-bolt anchor.
No bolts and no gear. Ends at a large tree or the top of the cliff. Loose or damp lichen and snapping crystals demand focus.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts up the bolted line of The Struggle Within, climbing a crack past its first four bolts, then steps right to the belay bolts beneath the second pitch of the East Wall route.
Bolted climbing that trends up and right to reach the arete followed by Eye of the Beholder. Pitches 1 and 2 can be linked on a 70 m rope if the rope is managed with long runners.
Easy natural-gear climbing at about 5.7 leads to one bolt-protected hard move, then a crack that widens up to a hanging belay. Pitches 3 and 4 can be linked on a 70 m rope with runners.
A wide crack taking 4-inch gear, then the line veers right to a bolted finish over a bulge. Belay on a ledge.
Easy bolted face climbing on imperfect rock up to an anchor. Pitches 5 and 6 can be linked on a 70 m rope.
A bolted face crosses a section of poor rock; the holds near the top are solid.

The finest climbing on the route, on solid rock near the top of the summit tower. Once at the arete, clip a bolt to protect the second, then move down and around the corner onto a ledge. The anchor there is not built for rappelling.
Move right to a water streak with bolts and stem up past questionable rock to a better finish. Belay on the slings or bolts just above the lip, or carry on to the summit and belay there.

pitch_detail.notes: P1 (5.11, about 50 m) scrambles up and right to a pedestal with one bolt; do not drift left toward the rap anchor, and belaying from the talus causes rope drag. P2 (5.11-, about 45 m) heads up and left, passes a rap anchor, then crosses blocky terrain to a tongue of clean rock; watch for loose blocks. P3 (5.12-, about 15 m) is a clean sculpted slab with a step-right crux, finishing on a sloping ledge under the overhanging Shield. Mostly less-than-vertical rock with some ledge scrambling.

P4 (5.12-, about 20 m) steps down right, then moves up jugs and trends left on exposed edges to a stance inside a dike; a straight-up direct variation is a closed project. P5 (5.13-, about 30 m) is the Dike pitch: the dike itself is about 5.11+, then a roughly V7 boulder crux on textureless pinches, then a 5.12 traverse right to a stance. P6 (5.11, about 30 m) is face climbing to a roof pull, then juggy sidepulls and edges to a corner belay.

P7 (5.12, about 30 m) follows a dihedral past a large rock scar, makes a hard step right on crimps, and rounds an arete to a sloping anchor stance before continuing through a roof to a second sloping stance; it is widely counted among the route's finest. P8 (5.12, about 15 m) is a corner of laybacking and stemming to an airy lip, with the belay in an alcove. The key pinch through the roof is the crux of this section.

P9 (5.11-, about 30 m) climbs a left-facing corner using face holds, the crack and a juniper, then pulls right to a stance. P10 (5.11+, about 35 m) is a tricky slab to a good ledge that is a poor one-person bivy but suits a portaledge (extra bolts were added for that). P11 (5.12, about 36 m) is under-vertical climbing to a layback crux and the right edge of a small roof, then easier ground past a rap anchor to a ledge under the Big Overhang; loose rock on that ledge.

P12 (5.13-, about 45 m) goes straight up through choss below a small roof, boulders through a second roof, then trends left through slopers (about V6) to a shallow corner, passes a rap anchor, and finishes with a redpoint boulder (about V5) over a bulge; permadraws are in place and about five more draws are needed. P13 (5.12, about 20 m) is sidepulls and compression blocks to a boulder move at the lip. P14 (5.11-, about 20 m) is jugs and pockets past suspect rock, and P15 (5.12, about 35 m) is bulgy ground on unusual holds to a slightly overhanging crimp crux, then jugs left and up to a belay below cedars. Stick clips or rodeo-clipping the permadraws help on the hard sections of P14 and P15.

P16 (5.8, about 65 m) puts hands on rock and feet on cedar trees up to a rap anchor, then a corner leads to a stance below a slab. P17 (5.9, about 70 m) is easy slab to a rock with a rap anchor, over it to cracks and trees, right to regain rock, then heather and trees, passing a rap anchor on a tree, to two bolts a little below the top of the buttress; a few feet of simul-climbing may be needed. Minimally cleaned, with loose rock on the ledges.

pitch_detail.notes: Where the lower ridge steepens into upper 5th class at a few trees, traverse left onto the more exposed side of the ridge. Find a snag beside a vertical #3-size crack. Climb cracks from the snag, including a short hand crack with 5.7 moves, to a belay just below the roof.

The 'Pac Man' pitch. Traverse out right under the roof, passing beneath its right side (going up and left over it is harder), and continue about 50 ft beyond. This pitch takes the most gear, and some parties find it the hardest. Above, scramble roughly ten minutes of class 3 up the ridge to the next steepening. The way on is not obvious here, and the gully alongside is loose.

Begin where the ground steepens and take the cracks, belaying wherever a stance suits or at the foot of a 10-inch-wide crack. Parties often link pitches 3 to 5 into two. Some belay 20–30 ft past the fixed rap anchors for better stances.
Short start up the 10-inch crack, with gear in cracks to its left. Above it, follow finger and hand cracks past a shallow gully and some bushes to a belay on a flat section.

Two options at the start: stay in the corner to the right the whole way, or take the middle cracks straight up to a tree. Either way, lieback the corner the tree grows in. Above the corner, easier ground leads to the next steepening of the ridge. Much of this pitch is easier than the others.
Follow cracks up to lower-angle ground and belay after about 140 ft, below the final headwall, which has a #3-size crack out to the left. Pitches 6 and 7 are the best-regarded on the route.

Short, excellent leaning crack on the left that starts at #3 size and gets smaller, the trickiest section of the route; only two or three pieces. The easier option is the blocky trough and gully to its right: walk a short ledge to an exposed step, then climb a second steep groove.

About 200–300 ft of class 3 along the crest, with an exposed 4th-class move near the summit. Topping out commits the party to descending the loose gully climber's right of the route. From the summit one rappel reaches that gully.

pitch_detail.notes: Dirty ledges lead to the first bolt, which is easiest to spot on the cleanest black-and-white granite. Follow the bolted slab up into a chute between two stands of trees and exit it to the right. Walk the belay uphill and left so the belayer sits under a right-facing corner.

Begin in the corner of brown, jagged rock that faces right, and stem up to a roof. Moves at the roof feel exposed, but the crux has good bolts. Above the roof, step right onto a short slab with bolts that ends at the anchor below a clean corner facing left. Some small optional gear helps above the slab crux.

The one pitch that takes no trad gear. Leave the belay on incut holds and climb the steep corner past the first roof (a brief move right, then back left onto the bolt line), and continue through the second overhang on white marbled rock. The top is a full-value arete: sustained face moves to the left, or bigger dynamic moves out right. A #1 or #2 cam is optional at the top. A first-time leader does well to clip the final hanger on the left and trend left. Stated length ranges from about 30 to 40 m.

Take the corner-ramp that slants right until it becomes an open book, with bolts visible ahead; ignore the extra bolt far out right on the arete unless taking that variation. After three bolts, head right along the arete to a bolted station on a small ledge facing the P5 crux across the way. Variation 1: step right off the belay with small gear to huge exposed fins, then go straight up to a four-inch slung horn and rejoin the normal line. Variation 2: from the slung horn, traverse right about 20 m on clean rock to the large gully, staying in the corner on its right side, to a gear belay a little right of the last bolted crux; protection is small gear plus .75, .3 and a 2 at the anchor, and it is a bit runout on easy ground.

Three bolts up a short, fun arete. Put a #1 cam in at the end of the overhang to protect the follower, then continue up and right to the bolted station where the wall ends. For the descent, look climber's left of this belay for a tree rappel anchor.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts at the top of the car-sized chockstone at the base of the east face. The first bolts are on slightly funky rock with yellow and orange lichen, but quality improves by the third bolt and the last five bolts are on superb granite. The climbing builds steadily on a steep, exposed face to a cryptic, steep crux (about V6) just below the anchor.

Almost no easy ground. The first half works up and around a vertical orange dike on interesting holds, leading into a short horizontal roof that needs blind reaches and heel hooks. Above the roof the angle eases only a little, with insecure moves to a small stance at the anchor.

An easier pitch before the crux. Leave the belay to the left, round the arete, and follow a brief, easy hand crack up to a bigger arete. A few moves are awkward and harder than they look, especially for shorter climbers.

The showpiece. Scramble left up the ramp to a little flake, climb past a few bolts of bouldery moves, then reach across right to where the finger crack begins. Layback and jam the roughly 45-foot crack to a good jug flake and rest. From there small feet and crimps lead over the bulge in a V9/V10 boulder problem, finished with a mantel onto a short slab. Without beta or chalk it can feel much harder than its grade.

Wander up the slab toward the big corner and the roof above it. Most of the pitch goes by jamming or laybacking on solid holds. It steepens before a traverse out and right around the offwidth roof; undercling and layback the offwidth until it is possible to squeeze inside, where feet and hands are good and the climbing quickly eases. A single #3 from the gear list is needed only on this pitch.

A short stretch of 4th class leads to a bolt by a tree, where the belay is moved. Climb left up a ramp, mantel up and right onto the top of a large flake, and set a few small cams before committing to insecure, awkward jams. The difficulty tapers off and better locks appear higher.
Straight up small ledges through some loose rock, a bit runout but never hard. Gain the huge open corner and turn right onto fun, easy laybacking.

Jam and stem up the overhanging open chimney on its left side until you can stem out to the right. Stay off the big wedged block close to the pitch's end, and build the belay on the bolts out left so the rope does not pinch behind that block.

A few wide stems up the chimney reach the first bolt; from there move left around the arete. Pleasant, easy face climbing trends up and left toward the arete separating the east face from the north, where the route meets Thin Red Line. Can be linked with pitch 10 if little gear is placed.

Easy ground over loose blocks, a little left of the arete, finishes the route. From here the choice is about 150 m of 4th-class terrain to the true summit, or rappelling the route on a single 80 m rope; the anchors on the route were placed roughly 40 m apart.

pitch_detail.notes: Low-angle, sometimes water-polished slab at 5.4-5.8, with runouts that can be long but on easy ground. The first two pitches link in one lead, and a competent party can run the next three and a half as a running belay to the top of the lower slabs. The pitch that reaches the first big ledge can be wet; a ramp on the left avoids it. P7 climbs a short 5.7 wall before easing back to slab. The whole route follows a gully slab, so anything knocked off above funnels straight down these pitches — the many bent hangers show it; do not linger below other parties.

A fun blocky ramp cutting through the steeper wall above the lower slabs, a full rope length from the base of that wall. Protection is sparse — two bolts of 5.7-5.8 at the start, a bolt about halfway and a fixed pin about 15 ft below the belay — but the climbing is easy. On the way down this ramp is downclimbed rather than rappelled.
The first 5.9 pitch, on steeper rock where the bolts are closer together as the moves get harder. It ends on a large ledge.
Easy climbing above the ledge. Skip the chain anchors and scramble to the foot of the steep wall to the left, belaying on a flake below the bolt line of the next pitch.
The first 5.10 pitch: well-bolted, balancy face climbing that is a fair test for the upper crux. Stay on the bolt line; forcing moves off it makes the pitch harder.
A more moderate pitch (roughly 5.8) up to chains. The top of this pitch makes a worthwhile objective on its own; above it the rock and climbing are poorer.

Easy (about 5.0-5.8) but the most runout section, on fair, slightly polished rock that sheds stones onto parties below. P13 is a full rope length with small cams useful in flakes, and can be run as one lead to a second set of chains up and right. A moderate pitch with five or six bolts follows to a belay where the wall kicks back. P15's two bolts are easy to miss and P16-17 have only the stations. Where the wall kicks back, go left to a bolt, up and right to a belay between a stand of trees and a heather patch (about 40 m, two bolts), then right along an obvious ramp of roughly 120 ft to the headwall; the trees and heather are useful landmarks on the descent too. Parties most often get lost here.
The first pitch of the upper headwall, where the bolt line picks back up, finishing on a tricky friction slab (around 5.9).

The crux: a steep, sustained wall nearly a full 60 m rope length, needing around 17 draws (bring long ones or back-clean). Its anchor has no chains; a chained station about 10 m higher lets two 60 m ropes reach the base of this pitch on the descent.
A chimney climbed by stemming and scrounging; it is often wet and can feel harder than the crux late in the day. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.
An easier, fun pitch up blocky ground, ending about 30 m below the summit.
A steep friction finish to the summit that looks easy from the belay but has few holds; well bolted and airy. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts at a tree well to the right of the arete proper. Easy, straightforward climbing leads to a good block stance. Parties traversing in from the Caves side rarely see the tree and rope up about 40 ft above it; make an intermediate belay there, because a flake catches the rope and makes belaying the second to the next start awkward.

The most sustained and serious pitch. The line is flaring and partly off-width. An old piton sits at the crux bulge but only protects once the move is made, so back it up with a small cam (about a 0.75) and be solid. The belay is a huge ledge. It is possible to escape right from here with two rappels (a 60 m rope was used; a 50 m rope may not reach without leaving gear).

The original line crosses back and forth over the arete on a roofy pitch through a black rock band, starting just left of the arete on a runout but easy face before returning to the right side. Fun face climbing with roof pulls that finishes at a good belay ledge. A committing 5.9 variant goes right off the ledge and works back left into the black band.

Traverse left; gear is available before moving around the arete, but a second's fall on the traverse swings out and off the arete. Then climb good holds up through the black rock and traverse back right across quartz on a delicate sequence of footholds. A fixed piece on the traverse is worn and worth backing up with a cam. The belay is on a sloping ledge, using a fixed pin plus gear in a seam. A sustained 5.8 variant stays right of the arete.

Climb cracks and face moves left of the sloping ledge to a horizontal knife-edge. Straight ahead of the belay, a steeper 5.9 crack running from fingers to hands cuts a short band of quartz, with jugs to help through an off-balance move and big exposure below. From the knife-edge, a short leapfrog gets you to a tree.

The standard way goes down and right roughly 150 ft into a gully and then up a weakness (about 5.5). The more direct line is a 5.8 hand and fist crack in front of the tree, with sustained fist jams and poor feet. A 5.9+ to 5.10a variant takes the arete crest more directly on the left, and a 5.9 option stays left of the arete. Belay on an easy slab.
Easy ground for a couple of hundred feet up and left, then back right. Soloing, simul-climbing or belaying all work. The walk-off appears obvious on the right.

pitch_detail.notes: The common start is the first three pitches of the neighbouring route Remorse, which keeps the overall grade at 5.9. It begins close to where the approach trail reaches the wall, climbing broken, blocky mid-fifth-class ground to a roomy ledge for the belay.
Climb cracks straight up a short way, then trend left to a thin flake and keep traversing left below it to a ledge belay.

A chimney and blocks lead to the ledge where Outer Space proper begins. The original easier start (5.7, one or two pitches that can be simul-climbed) instead goes up a left-trending corner and scramble and then traverses past a fixed sling to the large ledge with bushes; it is easy to lose the route here.

Start up a hard crack or the dihedral to its left, reach a roof, then step out right on the famous exposed finger traverse and follow the crack right until it heads up again. Protection is good but rope drag builds. Some of the flakes on the lower crack are hollow, and one key flake was thought to have been torn off in 2021, so check holds and gear. Belay on a sloping ledge.

Move left from the belay on an easy slab with knobs, then make exposed face moves to a right-facing dihedral forming the right side of a pedestal. The dihedral is the crux of the pitch. Top out, clip the bolt above, and traverse across to the pedestal's left side, belaying at the base of the splitter. It is longer than it looks and drags on the rope.

The standout pitch: a long splitter hand crack through the shield, with bomber jams and knobs on the face when the arms tire. Doubles or triples in hand sizes help avoid running out of gear. The pitch finishes on an ideal ledge, where a second crack takes the anchor.

A bouldery move leaves the ledge, then the crack continues as easy jamming to the top. Gear goes up to about 3.5 inches. A 70 m rope reaches the summit boulder, which takes small gear, but not the trees 30 ft further. Save small cams or bring the second up before the low-angle chickenhead finish; the last stretch to the top is about 50 ft of scrambling.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin in the corner below an orange panel facing east, where the buttress meets the ground. Climb a blocky weakness, make a strenuous move left to a dihedral on the lowest pillar, and follow a hand crack to a belay on a nice ledge atop the pillar. This is part of the three-pitch direct start that replaces the original first two pitches (5.6 and 5.8).

The physical and mental crux. Step left around the corner from the belay into a dihedral with blocks, make a bouldery move to a rail sticking out about a foot with a flake above it, then work left past an edge and traverse the face to a belay in the wide crack that splits the lower buttress. Sporty, gear-protected, with a serious feel.

Climb the steep splitter for about 35 m, step right to an obvious ledge, then follow a less strenuous corner to a pedestal at the top of the pillar with a large diving-board block. The belay takes medium nuts.

Pass a wide stretch and a ledge to reach the steep crack leaning right, sustained hands to fists, passing an old homemade hanger in the wall to the right of the crack. Follow the crack to its end, trend right over blocky terrain, and belay in blocks in the middle of the buttress. Aid on the first ascent.
Head up and left to a corner crack capped by a block that forms a keyhole. Belay under the block.
Go about 5 m left from the belay into a chimney system and make wide moves to a blocky exit onto the bivy ledge used by the first ascent party.

Several options leave the bivy ledge: a splitter crack on the left, a dihedral center-right, or a broken crack system trending right. The right option goes through a small roof to blocky terrain below the upper headwall. With a 70 m rope belay at the headwall base; with a 60 m rope belay short and scramble about 10 m of easy third class to the base.

The showpiece. Start in the perfect hand crack to the right of the off-width splitter. It widens a bit, then pinches to tight hands and ring locks before the wide crack joins it from the left. Bold moves reach a ledge with an old angle piton of doubtful quality; a #6 cam makes a convenient belay, otherwise use small gear and chockstones.

A flaky layback leads to small footholds, then a 10 m traverse right to a good vertical hand crack. Follow it to blocky terrain and belay in a corner at large blocks. Steep and bouldery in the dihedral, with excellent movement; aided at A2 originally. A second source rates it 5.10+ while the original route description gives 5.9, so treat the grade as a range.
Climb the short steep corner and the broken face just left of it to blocky, easier terrain that tops out the Aiguille. Walk off.

pitch_detail.notes: Start in the crack system about 30 ft left of the descent gully. Aid the crack past a false belay to the real one, roughly 130 ft up. Much of it would go free at a moderate grade. If aiding without back-cleaning, carry three each of #2 and #3 and two #4s.
Stay in the crack as it opens into a flared groove.
Follow the clear line up to a ledge where the Finger begins. Right off the belay, old pin scars and holes give short but tricky aid, and some free moves are mandatory and committing.

Traverse the ledge around the corner (about 5.6) to an ancient bolt, aid the tricky roof (about A2), and continue to a belay on the far side of the Finger. The traverse is protected by old drilled angles and a star drive; fixed tricams and fixed pins at the start of the roof are old and sketchy. A screamer helps for anchor falls. This gets you to the base of the Finger.
Scramble to a drilled pin, then climb the strenuous flare (aid C1, or free about 5.10). At its top, 5.8 grovelling is needed to reach the belay, which is on the ridge facing the Duck.
Go around the Duck on its left. The anchor for the descent rappels is on its far side. Keep following the wide cracks up to a big ledge, which is a bivy site, and belay there.

Move right around the arete to a seam and aid it (about A2) back to the crest. A mix of free climbing (5.7-5.8) and C2 aid on doubtful fixed gear reaches an exposed stance on the arete; placements and a fixed pin lead to many bolts to anchor.

Mixed free (5.7-5.8) and aid (C2, long reaches) past old fixed gear to a wide crack. Continue up it, over a roof in the caprock with wild exposure, and mantle to the belay. Nearly a bolt ladder, with free moves and top steps.
Fourth-class scrambling to the summit.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel to the top of pitch 7.
rappel_detail.station: Top of pitch 8, below the summit scramble.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel to the anchor beside the Duck at the top of pitch 6.
rappel_detail.station: Top of pitch 7, on the arete.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three double-rope rappels down the descent gully to the base.
rappel_detail.station: Next to the Duck, on the far side of the pitch 6 traverse.

rappel_detail.notes: Second double-rope rappel in the gully.
Third double-rope rappel to the base. To skip the walk around the tower, a shorter way down takes two double-rope rappels westward down the cliff close to the base.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble the fourth-class approach ramp (rope up if you might fall) to a large flat area, then start at a short fingertip crack. It is low and quick, with one good fingerlock to lunge for. Two ways reach the first ramp belay: a short right-facing dihedral then a traverse right, or a traverse right to the same ramp.

Reach the right-facing Ruper crack by traversing or downclimbing right about 30 ft. It is a roughly 5-inch crack at the back of a flaring dihedral; ripples for lips and feet keep it at 5.8. Bring a #3.5 or #4 cam, and use side cracks higher up. The Rover variation, up the block's left side, is easier than it looks but still about 5.9.

Begins with a wildly airy thin friction traverse over a slight bulge, then a fun dihedral to a big belay ledge, the Upper Ramp. Doubles help protect the follower on the traverse: clip only one rope while leading the dihedral so the other acts as a top rope. Rappelling off is possible after these first three pitches.

After a short fourth-class scramble, climb a short protectable dihedral, then work left onto runout 5.6 face climbing on solid, juggy rock. A fall in the wrong spot lands on the belay ledge. Belay on a tiny shelf.
A short pitch to a cramped pod under a huge roof. The anchor is two old pins backed up with a marginal cam between fractured blocks.

Traverse under the roof past three old pitons, with good cam and nut placements that should be used instead. A few reachy 5.8 moves past a hidden jug end the technical climbing, then about 40 ft of easy runout ground leads to a belay tree. The 5.8 move is poorly protected by two unreliable pins; the upper section is runout 5.5 and wet after rain or snow. A 15-minute scramble leads to the summit of Tower One.

pitch_detail.notes: A right-leaning crack system leads to the obvious roof; it is hard to miss. Most parties find this the hardest-feeling pitch, though the technical crux comes later. Fingertip to hand-size gear, doubles recommended.

Move out right beneath the roof and take the corner above it. The move under the roof is the technical crux and a small cam (a purple C3 was useful) protects it. The pitch ends at a long horizontal crack that takes a #3-size cam, where you belay on gear while standing in the crack. Parties often link this with the first half of the next pitch, or stop at a stance in the corner after linking pitch 1.

A slab leads to a short chimney exit. The chimney has loose rock, so one option is to skip it: take the ramp to its right and traverse left over the top into the easy corner. If you do climb it, follow the seam arcing left on the chimney's left wall. Linking this with the 5.8 above reaches a belay on a large ledge, and a 60 m rope often forces a stop before the looser 5.8 section.
Off-width to a mantle on an arching seam, ending on the large ledge at the foot of the last pitch. Often climbed together with pitch 3, in which case a 70 m rope links it more easily.

The aesthetic finishing corner: a perfect corner crack above the ledge, about 50 feet, with small gear and nuts useful at the start (tips to fingers), then move right to a little tree just under the West Ridge crest. With enough gear and good rope management you can carry on to the top of the ridge, then either rappel the back side or continue to the summit. Some rate this pitch softer than the earlier 5.11a.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin toward the west end of the south face, roughly 100 ft right of Solid Gold. A short crack leads to a low-angle slab below a corner; follow the corner to a belay under a steep white face. The route sees little traffic, so test the rock, which can be loose in places.

A long pitch up exposed, somewhat dirty face cracks that are lined with lichen, trending a bit leftward to a ledge below a sharp corner. The line wanders, so expect heavy rope drag by the top; extend runners generously. Climb carefully on the lichen.
The best pitch on the route. A fun bouldery move gets you into the clean corner, which you follow before exiting right into an alcove for the belay.

Starts with a finger crack on a slab (around 5.10b) that widens to hands before a step left into a flake. The crack can thin back to fingers above the hand section, so carry small cams and place them before the thin part. Finish up the last hand cracks (about 5.8) to the West Ridge, where several nearby south-face routes top out. The first-ascent party climbed this with nuts and hexes only.

rappel_detail.notes: A single 60 m rope reaches the ground. Scramble down to the notch under the West Ridge route, then back to the base of the south face, trending right for a while to avoid cliffs directly below the notch. About 30 minutes from the top of the route to its base.
rappel_detail.anchor: Rappel anchor on the north side of the ridge (shared with Solid Gold)
hazards: cliffs directly below the West Ridge notch on the scramble back
rappel_detail.station: From the top of the route, or after scrambling the West Ridge, find the rappel anchor on the north side of the ridge, the same one used after Solid Gold.
